title: Why the disciples faced death
source_text: Πρὸς τούτοις δὲ θαυμάσαι ἄν τις, πόθεν ἐπῆλθε τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ, ὡς λέγουσιν οἱ κακολογοῦντες τὸν Ἰησοῦν, μὴ ἑωρακόσιν αὐτὸν ἀναστάντα ἀπὸ τῶν νεκρῶν μηδὲ πεισθεῖσιν ὅτι θειότερόν τι ἦν ἐκεῖνος, πρὸς τῷ μὴ φοβηθῆναι τὰ αὐτὰ τῷ διδασκάλῳ παθεῖν καὶ ὁμόσε χωρῆσαι τῷ κινδύνῳ καὶ καταλιπεῖν τὰς πατρίδας ὑπὲρ τοῦ διδάξαι κατὰ τὸ Ἰησοῦ βούλημα τὸν παραδοθέντα αὐτοῖς ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ λόγον. οἶμαι γὰρ ὅτι ὁ εὐγνωμόνως ἐξετάζων πράγματα οὐκ ἂν λέγοι τούτους ἑαυτοὺς παραδεδωκέναι περιστατικῷ βίῳ ἕνεκεν τῆς Ἰησοῦ διδασκαλίας χωρίς τινος μεγάλης πειθοῦς, ἣν ἐνεποίησεν αὐτοῖς διδάσκων οὐ μόνον διακεῖσθαι κατὰ τὰ μαθήματα αὐτοῦ ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄλλους διατιθέναι, καὶ διατιθέναι προὔπτου ὄντος ὡς πρὸς τὸν ἀνθρώπων βίον ὀλέθρου τῷ τολμῶντι πανταχοῦ καὶ πρὸς πάντας καινοτομεῖν καὶ μηδένα ἀνθρώπων, ἐμμένοντα τοῖς προτέροις δόγμασι καὶ ἔθεσι, φίλον ἑαυτῷ τηρεῖν. ἆρα γὰρ οὐχ ἑώρων οἱ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μαθηταὶ, τολμῶντες οὐ μόνον Ἰουδαίοις ἐκ τῶν προφητικῶν λόγων παριστάνειν ὅτι οὗτος εἴη ὁ προφητευθεὶς, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς ἔθνεσιν ὅτι ὁ χθὲς καὶ πρώην σταυρωθεὶς ἑκὼν τοῦτον τὸν θάνατον ὑπὲρ τοῦ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένους ἀνεδέξατο, ἀνάλογον τοῖς ἀποθανοῦσιν ὑπὲρ πατρίδων ἐπὶ τῷ σβέσαι λοιμικὰ κρατήσαντα καταστήματα ἢ ἀφορίας ἢ δυσπλοΐας; εἰκὸς γὰρ εἶναι ἐν τῇ φύσει τῶν πραγμάτων κατά τινας ἀποῤῥήτους καὶ δυσλήπτους τοῖς πολλοῖς λόγους φύσιν τοιαύτην, ὡς ἕνα δίκαιον ὑπὲρ τοῦ κοινοῦ ἀποθανόντα ἑκουσίως ἀποτροπιασμοὺς ἐμποιεῖν φαύλων δαιμονίων, ἐνεργούντων λοιμοὺς ἢ ἀφορίας ἢ δυσπλοΐας ἤ τι τῶν παραπλησίων. λεγέτωσαν οὖν οἱ βουλόμενοι ἀπιστεῖν τῷ Ἰησοῦν ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων ἀποτεθνηκέναι τρόπῳ σταυροῦ, πότερον οὐδὲ τὰς Ἑλληνικὰς παραδέξονται καὶ βαρβαρικὰς πολλὰς ἱστορίας περὶ τοῦ τινας ὑπὲρ τοῦ κοινοῦ τεθνηκέναι καθαιρετικῶς τῶν προκαταλαβόντων τὰς πόλεις καὶ τὰ ἔθνη κακῶν· ἢ ἐκεῖνα μὲν γεγένηται οὐδὲν δὲ πιθανὸν ἔχει ὁ νομιζόμενος ἄνθρωπος πρὸς τὸ ἀποθανεῖν ἐπὶ καθαιρέσει μεγάλου δαίμονος καὶ δαιμόνων ἄρχοντος, ὑποτάξαντος ὅλας τὰς ἐπὶ γῆν ἐληλυθυίας ἀνθρώπων ψυχάς; ὁρῶντες δὲ ταῦτα οἱ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μαθηταὶ καὶ ἄλλα τούτων πλείονα, ἃ εἰκὸς αὐτοὺς ἐν ἀποῤῥήτῳ ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μεμαθηκέναι, ἔτι δὲ καὶ δυνάμεώς τινος πληρωθέντες. ἐπεὶ ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς μένος καὶ θάρσος οὐ ποιητική τις παρθένος ἀλλ᾿ ἡ ἀληθῶς φρόνησις καὶ σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ, (ἔσπευσαν,) ἵν᾿ ἔκδηλοι μετὰ πᾶσιν οὐ μόνοις Ἀργείοις γένοιντο ἀλλὰ καὶ πᾶσιν Ἕλλησιν ὁμοῦ καὶ βαρβάροις, καὶ κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἄροιντο.
pass_a_gloss: Besides these, one might wonder whence it came upon (ἐπέρχομαι) his disciples - as Jesus' revilers say, not having seen him risen (ἀνίστημι) from the dead nor persuaded (πείθω) that he was something more divine (θειότερον) - not to fear to suffer the same as the teacher, and to go to close quarters (ὁμόσε χωρέω) with danger, and to leave their fatherlands in order to teach, according to Jesus' will (βούλημα), the word handed over (παραδίδωμι) to them by him. For I think one examining fairly (εὐγνωμόνως) would not say these gave themselves to a life beset with dangers (περιστατικὸς βίος) for Jesus' teaching without some great persuasion (πειθώ), which he implanted (ἐμποιέω) in them, teaching not only to be disposed (διάκειμαι) according to his lessons (μαθήματα) but also to dispose (διατίθημι) others, and to dispose [them] when destruction (ὄλεθρος) was foreseen/in plain view (πρόοπτος), as regards human life, for one daring everywhere and toward all to innovate (καινοτομέω) and to keep as friend no man abiding in the former doctrines and customs. For did not Jesus' disciples see, daring to present (παριστάνω) not only to Jews from prophetic words that this was the one prophesied, but also to the other nations that the one crucified yesterday and the day before (χθὲς καὶ πρώην) willingly (ἑκών) accepted (ἀναδέχομαι) this death for the race of men, analogously to those who died for fatherlands to quench (σβέννυμι) pestilential conditions (λοιμικὰ καταστήματα) that prevailed, or barrenness/famines (ἀφορίαι), or bad voyages (δυσπλοΐαι)? For it is likely that there is in the nature of things, according to certain secret (ἀπόρρητοι) reasons (λόγοι) hard to grasp for the many, such a nature that one righteous man (εἷς δίκαιος) dying willingly for the common (τὸ κοινόν) produces avertings (ἀποτροπιασμοί) of evil demons (φαῦλα δαιμόνια) working plagues (λοιμοί) or famines or bad voyages or something similar. Let those wishing to disbelieve that Jesus died for men by way of a cross (σταυρός) say whether they will not accept even the many Greek and barbarian histories (ἱστορίαι) about some having died for the common, destructively (καθαιρετικῶς) of evils that had seized beforehand cities and nations; or those things happened, but the one supposed a man (ὁ νομιζόμενος ἄνθρωπος) has nothing credible (πιθανόν) toward dying for the destruction (καθαίρεσις) of a great demon (δαίμων) and ruler of demons (δαιμόνων ἄρχων), who had subjected (ὑποτάσσω) all the souls of men come to earth? Seeing these and other things more than these, which they likely learned in secret (ἐν ἀπορρήτῳ) from Jesus, and moreover filled with a certain power (δύναμις), since not some poetic maiden (παρθένος) but the true prudence (φρόνησις) and wisdom (σοφία) of God gave them might (μένος) and courage (θάρσος), [they hastened] that they might become conspicuous (ἔκδηλοι) among all, not only Argives but all Greeks together and barbarians, and win noble fame (κλέος ἐσθλόν).
pass_b_english: Besides this, one might wonder what moved his disciples, if, as those who speak evil of Jesus say, they had not seen him risen from the dead and had not been persuaded that he was something more divine, not to fear suffering the same things as their teacher, and to meet the danger head-on and leave their homelands to teach, as Jesus willed, the word he had entrusted to them (see Matthew 28:19–20). For I think that anyone who examines the facts fairly would not say that these men gave themselves up to a life full of dangers for the sake of Jesus’ teaching without some great conviction. He had planted it in them by teaching them not only to be shaped by his teachings themselves but also to shape others by them, and to do so when ruin, as far as human life goes, lay in plain view for anyone who dared to bring in new things everywhere and with everyone, and to keep as a friend no one who held fast to his former doctrines and customs.

Did Jesus’ disciples not see this, when they dared to show not only the Jews, from the words of the prophets, that he was the one foretold, but also the other nations that the man crucified only the other day had willingly accepted this death for the human race, like those who died for their countries to put an end to plagues that had taken hold, or famines, or disasters at sea? For it is likely that in the nature of things there is, for certain secret reasons hard for most people to grasp, an order such that one righteous man, dying willingly for the common good, brings about the driving away of evil demons, who cause plagues or famines or disasters at sea or something of the kind.

Let those, then, who wish to disbelieve that Jesus died for mankind by way of the cross tell us: will they also refuse to accept the many Greek and barbarian stories of people who died for the common good, to destroy evils that had already seized cities and nations? Or will they say that those things did happen, but that there is nothing credible in the one they take to be a man dying to destroy a great demon, the ruler of demons, who had made subject to himself all the souls of men that have come to earth?

Jesus’ disciples saw these things, and many more besides, which they are likely to have learned from Jesus in private. They were filled, moreover, with a certain power, since the one who gave them “strength and courage” was not some maiden of the poets but the true understanding and wisdom of God. So they hastened to become “conspicuous among all,” not only among the Argives but among all Greeks and barbarians alike, “and to win noble fame” (Homer, Iliad 5.1–3).

choices.choice: The last sentence adapts Homer, Iliad 5.1–3 (Pallas Athena gives Diomedes 'strength and courage, that he might be conspicuous among all the Argives and win noble fame'); the 'maiden of the poets' is Athena. (ἔσπευσαν) 'they hastened' is an editor's supplement, followed. 'Did Jesus' disciples not see this': ἑώρων has no stated object; 'this' (the ruin just mentioned) is supplied for English sense; one could instead take the following 'that he willingly accepted death' as part of what they saw. 'To teach, as Jesus willed' is taken as a clear allusion to the commission in Matthew 28:19–20. Possible but uncited allusions, kept out of the reading text: 'one righteous man dying for the common good' (compare John 11:50; 1 Peter 3:18); his death 'to destroy ... the ruler of demons' (compare Hebrews 2:14; John 12:31); 'the true understanding and wisdom of God' may point to Christ as the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), so kept lower case. δυσπλοΐαι ('bad voyages', failed sailings) rendered 'disasters at sea'. ὁ νομιζόμενος ἄνθρωπος rendered 'the one they take to be a man' (that is, a mere man). ἢ ἐκεῖνα μὲν γεγένηται ... is the second option the opponents are asked to state (governed by λεγέτωσαν), so it is rendered 'Or will they say that ...'.

First sentence restructured: πόθεν ἐπῆλθε ... πρὸς τῷ μὴ φοβηθῆναι -> 'one might wonder what moved his disciples ... not to fear', replacing the stiff 'where it came from in his disciples ... that they did not fear'
παραδοθέντα: 'handed down' (suggests later tradition) -> 'entrusted to them'
καινοτομεῖν καὶ ... τηρεῖν: removed the added consequence 'and so'; both infinitives now depend on 'dared'; πρὸς πάντας -> 'with everyone'
ἢ ἐκεῖνα μὲν γεγένηται: turned from a stray question ('Or did those things happen') into the opponents' second option ('Or will they say that those things did happen, but ...')
Checked Matthew 28:19–20 (commission to teach) and Homer, Iliad 5.1–3 (μένος καὶ θάρσος, ἔκδηλος, κλέος ἐσθλόν)
